rv.q: This is a musical that dares to examine the toll that mental illness takes on a family, and it does so with a rare combination of honesty, insight and artistry.
The show's emotional authenticity and Brian Yorkey's intelligent book make 'Next to Normal' a landmark musical about mental illness that doesn't shrink from the subject's complexity.
The show is an impressive achievement, a heartfelt entertainment.
The show succeeds in making audiences care deeply about these characters while never minimizing the devastating impact of mental illness on families.

What makes 'Next to Normal' exceptional is that it treats mental illness not as a metaphor for the human condition but as a disease whose effects on both patients and their families are explored with clinical precision and unsparing honesty.
This bracingly honest musical about a family coping with mental illness boasts a brilliant performance from Alice Ripley and a superb score by Tom Kitt and Brian Yorkey.
"Next to Normal" still has issues -- the aimless second act remains stuck in a circling pattern -- but now it's acquired an intriguing dimension as social commentary.
The brilliant star of this show is the show itself.
As directed by Michael Greif, the production is both emotionally charged and intellectually challenging, making for a near perfect evening at the theater.

cn.t: Critics largely praise this ambitious rock musical about mental illness for its emotional authenticity and unflinching honesty, though some find it easier to admire than love despite extensive retooling that improved the show.

sg.ra: The Booth is one of Broadway's smallest houses at 766 seats, so center orchestra rows C-H give close-up detail of plays and intimate dramas without paying the very-front premium. Row AA front offers max legroom (Headout) but stage is high; step back a few rows for better sightline onto the stage floor.

sg.vl: Workable angle, not the sweet spot
sg.ra: Booth is narrow so side orchestra remains viable, but a 2018 BWW forum post specifically flagged 'angle from the front side seats' as a concern. Closer rows (BB, A) on the side get awkward angles onto the high stage. Mid-house aisle seats recover the view while adding legroom.
sg.rr: A-P (17 rows, odd 1-15 left, even 2-16 right)

sg.ra: In a 252-seat mezzanine with only 8 rows, even the back row is close. SeatPlan and Headout both call Center Mezz A-B some of the best seats in the house, and G-H are cited as strong value. With the Booth's intimate scale, the mezzanine never feels distant — this is the value pick.

sg.vl: Small house saves the side angle
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly notes side-mezz views are 'slightly more angled but still viable' because the Booth is narrow. Decent budget alternative, but the center mezz is a better value at similar price tier so this is solid-not-sweet.
